issues.legal_issue: A resulting trust does not arise when the settlor manifested a contrary intention for the property on failure or revocation of the trust.
material_facts: The trust was created by statute at the settlor’s instance and was treated as a private trust.
The settlor’s will provided for his sons other than the eldest, who was to receive the trust’s benefits as the succeeding title-holder.
The will gave the eldest son a special position and contemplated that his line would supply future title-holders.
The trust instrument provided that, in the specified ultimate contingency, the property would go to the heirs of the last title-holder.
issues.conclusion: The settlor’s contrary intention was established; no resulting trust arose in favour of his estate, and the trust property was intended to pass to the last title-holder and his heirs.
issues.legal_principle: Section 83 of the Indian Trusts Act provides for a resulting trust in the absence of a contrary direction. The contrary intention may be inferred from the instrument and admissible surrounding circumstances; the Court relied on Cock v Hutchinson, King v Dinison, Hill v Bishop of London, and the discussion in Scott on Trusts.

predicates.private_trust_failure_or_revocation_case: The dispute concerns property held in a private trust that has failed or been revoked.
predicates.settlor_manifested_contrary_intention_fo: The settlor’s instrument and surrounding circumstances show that the property was intended to pass to someone other than the settlor or the settlor’s estate if the trust failed or was revoked.

issues.definition: When a private trust fails or is revoked and the settlor manifested a contrary intention for the property, the property passes as the settlor intended rather than under a resulting trust.

issues.legal_issue: A distribution provision requires transfer of trust property to the custodian when the person entitled to it was declared an evacuee and that person’s interest in the property was declared evacuee property.
material_facts: After repeal of the trust statute, the Official Trustee sought directions for distributing the trust property among claimants.
The succeeding title-holder was found entitled to the trust property.
That title-holder had been declared an evacuee, and his beneficial interest in the trust property had been declared evacuee property.
The repealing legislation directed the Official Trustee to transfer and vest qualifying property in the Custodian.
issues.conclusion: Because all three conditions were satisfied, the Official Trustee was required to transfer and vest in the Custodian the trust property found to be evacuee property, subject to applicable court directions and prior payment of established liabilities and expenses.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 7(4) of the repealing legislation, the required conditions are that a person is entitled to the trust property or part of it, has been or is declared an evacuee under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and has had their interest in the trust property declared evacuee property under that Act. The Court read “evacuee property” consistently with section 2(f) of the 1950 Act and held that section 7(4) supplied a separate statutory route for vesting qualifying property in the Custodian.

rule.if: trust_property_distribution_proceeding and person_entitled_to_trust_property and person_declared_evacuee and person's_interest_declared_evacuee_property

predicates.trust_property_distribution_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding to determine the distribution of property held by a trust that has been repealed or revoked.
predicates.person_entitled_to_trust_property: A person has been found entitled to the trust property or a part of it.
predicates.person_declared_evacuee: The person has been declared an evacuee under the applicable evacuee-property law.
predicates.person's_interest_declared_evacuee_prope: The person’s right, title, and interest in the trust property has been declared evacuee property under the applicable evacuee-property law.

issues.definition: In a trust-property distribution proceeding, if the person entitled to property has been declared an evacuee and that person’s interest has been declared evacuee property, the Official Trustee must transfer the qualifying property to the Custodian.

issues.legal_issue: A state law providing for custody, management, or disposal of evacuee property is not invalid for lack of legislative competence or repugnancy when it is within the relevant legislative field and operates as additional, non-conflicting legislation with presidential assent.
material_facts: The State Legislature enacted the repealing and distribution legislation, which provided for vesting qualifying trust property in the Custodian.
The legislation received the President’s assent.
The Court found that the provision was additional legislation on evacuee property and was not repugnant to the central evacuee-property law.
issues.conclusion: The provision was within the State Legislature’s competence and was not invalid on the ground of repugnancy.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Entries 41 and 27 of the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule and Article 254(2) of the Constitution. It held that the provision was additional legislation concerning evacuee property, did not conflict with the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and had received the President’s assent.

predicates.state_legislature_enacted_evacuee_proper: A State Legislature enacted a law providing for custody, management, or disposal of property belonging to evacuees.
predicates.presidential_assent_given: The President assented to the State law.
predicates.provision_adds_to_existing_law_without_c: The provision supplies an additional means of dealing with evacuee property and does not conflict with the existing central law on that subject.

issues.definition: A state evacuee-property provision enacted within the relevant legislative field, given presidential assent, and operating without conflict with existing law withstands competence and repugnancy challenges.

issues.legal_issue: The death of a title-holder does not transfer the trust benefit to that holder’s heirs when the benefit passes under the trust succession arrangement to the succeeding title-holder.
material_facts: The trust provided benefits to the title-holder for the time being.
The third title-holder died, and his son succeeded to the title as the fourth title-holder.
The trust benefit passed to the succeeding title-holder.
issues.conclusion: The trust property did not devolve on the deceased title-holder’s widow and other heirs; the benefit passed to the succeeding title-holder.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the succession arrangement in the Baronetcy Act, under which the benefit of the trust passed to the title-holder for the time being and, on the prior title-holder’s death, to his successor.

predicates.trust_benefit_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to a trust benefit after the death of a title-holder.
predicates.trust_benefit_attached_to_current_title_: The trust arrangement grants the benefit to the title-holder for the time being.
predicates.successor_assumed_title_after_holder_die: After the title-holder died, a successor assumed the title under the applicable succession arrangement.

issues.definition: When a trust benefit belongs to the title-holder for the time being and a successor assumes the title after that holder’s death, the benefit passes to the successor rather than the deceased holder’s heirs.
